title: Podman Desktop consumes increasing CPU and memory while idle on Windows
body: I updated Podman and Podman Desktop on my Windows 11 machine, and Podman Desktop 1.14.2 installed through Scoop now consistently uses 20–30% CPU and up to 4 GB of memory while doing nothing. I have no images or containers in use. After it has been running for a while, the UI becomes almost unresponsive and sluggish, and my PC's fans run at full speed. Is this expected?

symptoms_visible: While I am doing nothing in Podman Desktop, its CPU stays around 20–30% and its memory grows as high as 4 GB.
After a while the UI becomes almost unresponsive, the whole application is sluggish, and my PC's fans run at full speed.
N0.label: N0 idle resource growth reported

symptoms_visible: Podman Desktop's memory and CPU usage still grow while the WSL-based Podman machine is running, even though the machine itself shows very low CPU usage.
N1.label: N1 environment and idle machine established

symptoms_visible: During Process Monitor tracking, Podman Desktop grew from about 300 MB toward 1 GB and continued consuming CPU.
The logs repeatedly print that the podman-machine-default pipe does not exist and that event handling will reconnect in five seconds.
The same CPU and memory growth returns after restarting Podman Desktop, WSL2, or the PC.
N2.label: N2 repeated connection errors captured

symptoms_visible: With every extension disabled, the resource problem does not occur.
When I enable only the Podman extension and start the Podman machine, the repeated errors return and CPU and memory pressure increase until the application becomes unbearable to use.
N3.label: N3 Podman extension path isolated

symptoms_visible: The Podman machine reports 100% idle CPU, about 554 MiB used memory, and no swap use while the Windows application has the problem.
Disabling the Windows firewall does not change the repeated errors or the increasing host CPU and memory use.
A second updated laptop also reaches almost 4 GB of memory and about 40% CPU after several hours.
N4.label: N4 VM load and firewall ruled out

symptoms_visible: After reverting Podman Desktop to 1.13.3, the repeated pipe errors and high CPU and memory use remain.
N5_x.label: N5_x Podman Desktop downgrade aftermath

symptoms_visible: After reverting Podman from 5.3.1 to 5.2.5, the repeated pipe errors stop and Podman Desktop no longer consumes increasing CPU or memory while idle.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved by Podman downgrade

question_patterns: Is the Podman virtual machine running while this happens?
Do you have a Podman machine active when the CPU and memory start growing?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes, the Podman VM is running.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: No, I have never initialized or started a Podman machine, and the problem starts immediately when I open the desktop application.

question_patterns: Is the Podman machine using WSL or Hyper-V?
How is the Podman machine configured?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It is using WSL, and I configured the machine in rootless mode.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It uses WSL in rootful mode instead of rootless mode.

question_patterns: Do you have Kind, Docker, OpenShift Local, or an active Kubernetes context running?
Is any other container or Kubernetes environment active?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I have nothing else running: no Kind, no Docker, no OpenShift Local, and no Kubernetes cluster.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Yes, Podman Desktop is connected to several active Kubernetes clusters and the resource use stops when I remove those contexts.
I have Docker installed, but it is stopped and removing it does not change the behavior.

edges.comment: Opening reporter's environment only, from c0-c4: the Podman VM is running through WSL in rootless mode; no other container or Kubernetes environment is active. The reporter additionally volunteered that top inside the machine was quiet.

question_patterns: Can you monitor the Podman Desktop process for a while and report how its resource use changes?
Could you capture a Process Monitor trace while the memory and CPU increase?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tracked it with Process Monitor. It kept growing from around 300 MB toward 1 GB before I stopped the trace, and it seemed to spend most of its time reading app.asar. I uploaded the PML.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The process remains stable near 300 MB for several hours and the slowdown comes entirely from the WSL VM.

question_patterns: Can you check the Podman Desktop logs for errors while the resource usage grows?
Please share the repeated log messages from the period of high CPU and memory use.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The logs repeatedly say `connect ENOENT \\.\pipe\podman-machine-default`, `Error when handling events`, and `Will reconnect in 5s`. They also occasionally say the engine has no API or libpod API and that it cannot get the machine's resource usage.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The logs remain quiet with no connection failures or repeated retries while memory grows.
The same ENOENT and reconnect messages repeat every ten seconds rather than every five seconds.

edges.comment: Opening reporter's system, c6-c15: after being asked for logs, the reporter supplied a Process Monitor trace and raw repeated ENOENT/reconnect lines. The conclusion that repeated connection handling may retain Dockerode instances was participant1's hypothesis, not the reporter's answer. The reporter later volunteered that application, WSL, and machine restarts do not prevent recurrence.

question_patterns: Could you disable all extensions and see whether CPU and memory still increase?
Does the issue reproduce with every extension disabled?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: When everything is disabled, I do not get the problem.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It still reaches the same CPU and memory usage with every extension disabled.

question_patterns: Can you enable the extensions one at a time and report which configuration reproduces the issue?
What happens with only the Podman extension enabled?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With only the Podman extension enabled, starting the Podman machine brings back all the log errors, and CPU and memory pressure increase until it becomes unbearable.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The Podman extension alone is fine; the issue appears only when I enable a different extension.
The same behavior occurs with only the Podman extension enabled, but it takes two hours instead of thirty minutes.

edges.comment: Opening reporter's extension-isolation test from c17-c18. This isolates the original issue to activity triggered by the Podman extension and running machine; it does not establish the later Kubernetes/Azure CLI problem reported by participant5.

question_patterns: Can you run `podman machine ssh top -b -n 1` and `podman machine ssh free -h` while checking the machine's CPU and memory?
What resource usage does the Podman machine itself report?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The machine reports 100% idle CPU. It has about 554 MiB used out of 7.7 GiB, about 7.2 GiB available, and no swap in use.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The machine itself is using all available CPU and nearly all of its memory when the desktop becomes sluggish.
The machine is 99% idle and uses about 700 MiB rather than 554 MiB.

question_patterns: Could a firewall be interfering with communication to the machine?
Can you temporarily disable the firewall and report whether the behavior changes?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I disabled the firewall, and it made no difference.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Disabling the firewall immediately stops the connection errors and resource growth.

edges.comment: Opening reporter's machine and firewall probes from c20-c23. The commands return raw VM statistics, while the host application still shows the issue. The same reporter also volunteered that a second updated laptop exhibited the same repeated errors and long-term growth.

solution.intent: Treat the regression as a Podman Desktop application-version problem and revert Podman Desktop to an earlier release.
solution.concrete_example: Revert Podman Desktop from the updated release to 1.13.3, leave the Podman engine unchanged, and monitor the logs and idle resource usage.

edges.comment: Opening reporter's actual failed attempt in c24: reverting Podman Desktop to 1.13.3 while leaving the newer Podman engine installed made no difference. This is distinct from participant4's later setup.

solution.intent: Treat the original report as a regression associated with the newer Podman engine's interaction with Podman Desktop: roll Podman back to the prior working engine build, then verify that the pipe-error retry loop and idle resource growth stop.
solution.concrete_example: Keep Podman Desktop installed, revert Podman from 5.3.1 to the previously working 5.2.5 build, restart the stack, and monitor both the logs and idle CPU/memory. On the reporter's system, the ENOENT messages stopped and the resource growth disappeared.
solution.inference_hint: The raw evidence establishes a repeated ENOENT/reconnect loop only when the Podman extension interacts with the running machine, while the VM itself is idle. Combining that with the failed Podman Desktop rollback and successful Podman engine rollback supports a Podman-version interaction on the host side. The thread only hypothesizes that repeatedly created Dockerode instances may evade garbage collection, so that specific memory-retention mechanism must not be presented as proven.

edges.comment: Resolution for the opening reporter from c24: reverting the Podman engine from 5.3.1 to 5.2.5 stopped both the repeated errors and the CPU/memory consumption. Comments c32-c36 describe participant5's separate Kubernetes/Azure CLI Python-spawn problem and are intentionally excluded from this causal chain.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the opening reporter's accepted diagnosis as a regression in the newer Podman engine's interaction with Podman Desktop, evidenced by the repeated missing named-pipe errors and five-second reconnection loop while the Podman machine itself remains idle.

Must ground the diagnosis in the collected evidence: quiet VM statistics, reproduction with only the Podman extension enabled, repeated ENOENT/reconnect logs, no effect from disabling the firewall, and no effect from reverting only Podman Desktop.
Must recommend rolling the Podman engine back to the prior working build, rather than claiming that downgrading Podman Desktop alone fixes the issue.
Must not present restarts, firewall changes, or a Podman Desktop-only downgrade as the resolution; they did not stop the original reporter's symptoms.

Must not conflate the opening report with the later participant's independent Kubernetes-context and Azure CLI Python-process problem or score toggling that participant's experimental feature as the original reporter's fix.
Must ask the reporter to verify that the repeated pipe errors and long-term idle CPU and memory growth are gone before declaring the issue resolved.
May describe uncollected Dockerode instances as a hypothesis only, not as a proven memory-leak mechanism.

persona_hint.experience_level: Technically capable Windows user who can inspect WSL and Podman machine state, run PowerShell and Linux diagnostic commands, capture Process Monitor traces, inspect application logs, isolate extensions, and downgrade installed packages.
persona_hint.communication_style: Persistent, cooperative, and evidence-oriented; provides raw logs and command output, tests suggested hypotheses, reports long-duration behavior, and clearly distinguishes observations from conclusions.
